methodology_notes: Each gate-passing benchmark was assessed by reading the vault paper YAML frontmatter, abstract, and PDF extract (first ~80 lines). Scores reflect what the benchmark actually tests based on primary source reading, not what the feature matrix claims.

assessments.filename: 2025-Multiple Journal of King Saud University-Leveraging Large Language Models for Detecting.md
assessments.extract_mismatch_note: PDF extract contains a DIFFERENT paper about SMS spam detection (Ahmadi et al.), NOT the ELQV Quran emotion paper. Assessment based on vault abstract and paper metadata only.

features.B3_note: Treats Islam as single tradition; dataset is Quranic verses only, no denominational variation

assessments.assessor_notes: This is a sentiment/emotion classification dataset for Quran verses, NOT a religious values benchmark. It tests whether models can detect emotions (fear, joy, anger, sadness) in Classical Arabic scripture. The low inter-annotator agreement (kappa 0.29-0.35) is concerning. Does not test religious values, ethical reasoning, or theological knowledge -- it tests emotion recognition in sacred text. A3 rated low because emotion detection is tangential to religious values alignment. CRITICAL: PDF extract is for a completely different paper (SMS spam detection).

assessments.short_title: Building Domain-Specific LLMs Faithful to the Islamic Worldview

features.B3_note: Focuses exclusively on Sunni orthodox Islam grounded in Quran and Sunnah; no denominational variation discussed

assessments.assessor_notes: This is a position/proposal paper from NeurIPS 2023 Muslims in ML Workshop, not a completed benchmark. It frames the problem of building LLMs faithful to Islamic worldview and proposes evaluation approaches but does not implement a complete benchmark. It discusses RAG with Islamic corpora, RLAIF for Islamic values, and evaluation by Islamic scholars. The actual benchmark/dataset is not yet fully realized -- it is more of a research agenda. Moderate A3 because the paper genuinely engages with Islamic values alignment as its core question.

assessments.filename: 2025-Kabir-Break the Checkbox Challenging Closed-Style Evaluations of Cultural.md
assessments.short_title: Break the Checkbox: Cultural Alignment Evaluation

features.B3_note: Religion appears only as one WVS demographic variable among many; no theological depth

assessments.assessor_notes: This paper critiques closed-style MCQ evaluation of cultural alignment (WVS, Hofstede). Religion is treated as a demographic variable in cross-cultural surveys, not as a theological construct. The paper's contribution is methodological (showing open-ended evaluation is better than forced-choice), not religious values assessment. A3 is low because religious values are incidental -- the paper is about evaluation methodology for cultural alignment broadly, and religion is just one of many cultural dimensions captured by WVS.

assessments.filename: 2023-Huang-AceGPT Localizing Large Language Models in Arabic.md

features.B3_note: Arabic culture and Islamic values treated as unified construct; no denominational variation

assessments.assessor_notes: AceGPT is primarily a localized Arabic LLM, not a religious values benchmark. Its evaluation includes Arabic cultural alignment via RLAIF with a reward model attuned to local culture and values. Religion is embedded within Arabic cultural context but is not the primary evaluation target. The paper conflates Arabic language competence, cultural knowledge, and Islamic values. A3 moderate because the paper explicitly addresses value alignment in Islamic cultural contexts, but the benchmark itself measures general Arabic NLP performance more than theological values.

assessments.short_title: Semantic and Sentiment Analysis of Bhagavad Gita

features.B3_note: Focuses on Bhagavad Gita only; mentions Vedanta but no denominational diversity
features.Q1_metric: Hand-labeled sentiment dataset mentioned but no IAA metrics reported

assessments.assessor_notes: This is a computational linguistics study comparing English translations of the Bhagavad Gita using BERT for sentiment and semantic analysis. It does NOT test religious values -- it tests whether different translations convey similar semantic content and sentiment. The theological concepts (Brahman, karma, dharma) appear in the text being analyzed but are not themselves being evaluated. The paper explicitly notes the absence of a Hindu philosophy BERT model. A3 is moderate because the sacred text content is inherently value-laden, but the benchmark itself measures translation quality, not values comprehension.

features.B3_note: Covers three monotheistic religions but with no intra-tradition nuance
features.Q1_metric: Annotation scheme with multiple annotators; specific metric not captured in first 80 lines

assessments.assessor_notes: This is a hate speech detection dataset, NOT a religious values benchmark. It tests whether models can detect abusive language targeting religious groups (Judaism, Christianity, Islam) on Twitter. Religion is the TARGET of hate speech, not the subject of values assessment. The benchmark has a fine-grained taxonomy of hate speech types and a bilingual (English/Italian) dataset. A3 is very low because detecting hate speech ABOUT religions is categorically different from testing alignment WITH religious values. High A4 (bias-values conflation) because this is purely bias detection masquerading as religious relevance.

features.B3_note: Only Sunni hadith collections; no Shia perspectives
features.Q1_metric: Verified by religious experts (specific metric unknown)

assessments.assessor_notes: Tests transformer models on detecting semantic relatedness between Quran verses and Hadith teachings. This is a text understanding task in Classical Arabic, not a values assessment. The dataset was curated by religious experts which adds quality, but the task itself (detecting relatedness between sacred texts) is primarily linguistic/semantic, not values-based. A3 moderate because understanding intertextual relationships in Islamic scripture has indirect relevance to values comprehension. No PDF extract available.

assessments.short_title: PapersPlease: Moral Dilemmas via ERG Theory

features.B3_note: Religion is just one social identity variable among many (gender, race, nationality, etc.); no theological content

assessments.assessor_notes: PapersPlease is a moral dilemma benchmark using ERG (Existence, Relatedness, Growth) motivational theory, framed as immigration inspector scenarios. Religion appears only as a social identity variable (e.g., testing if Muslim applicants get different approval rates than Christian ones). It does NOT test religious values or theological reasoning -- it tests bias in moral decision-making when religious identity is mentioned. A3 is low because the benchmark has zero religious VALUES content; religion is purely a demographic cue for bias detection. High V2 because the benchmark does genuinely test ethical reasoning, just not religiously-grounded reasoning.

features.B3_note: Religion is one sociodemographic variable among many; no theological engagement
features.Q1_metric: Individualised ratings linked to participant profiles; no traditional IAA

assessments.assessor_notes: PRISM is a large-scale participatory alignment dataset mapping 1,500 diverse participants from 75 countries to their feedback on 8,011 LLM conversations. Religion appears as one sociodemographic variable. The dataset targets subjective and multicultural perspectives on value-laden topics, but is not specifically about religious values. The paper explicitly addresses the 'whose values' question in alignment but treats religion as demographic, not theological. A3 is low because religious values are incidental to the broader alignment framework. Strong on V8 (normative pluralism) because the design explicitly accepts multiple valid perspectives.

assessments.short_title: HAQA and QUQA: Arabic QA Corpora for Quran and Hadith

features.B3_note: Sunni hadith collections; no denominational variation
features.Q1_metric: Expert-curated from religious scholars but no formal IAA

assessments.assessor_notes: HAQA (1,598 QA pairs on Hadith) and QUQA (3,382 QA pairs on Quran) are Arabic question-answering datasets for Islamic texts. This is primarily a knowledge retrieval task -- can a system find the correct answer from sacred texts? The questions are factual (who, what, where from Quran/Hadith), not values-based. A3 is moderate because the content domain is inherently religious and some questions may touch on ethical/jurisprudential topics, but the task format is knowledge recall, not values reasoning. Higher A3 than ELQV because the QA format can engage doctrinal content directly.

assessments.short_title: Quantifying Religious Bias in Open LLMs (Asian Nations)

features.B3_note: Religions treated as demographic categories; no theological nuance

assessments.assessor_notes: This paper measures religious BIAS in LLMs using Hamming distance from survey respondents in South/Southeast Asian countries. It uses Pew Research surveys on religious tolerance/identity. The method reveals which demographic profile an LLM most closely matches. Religion is treated purely as a demographic variable -- the paper asks 'does the LLM sound like a Hindu in India or a Muslim in Pakistan?' not 'does the LLM understand Hindu or Islamic values?' A3 is moderate because the surveys themselves contain values-relevant questions about religious tolerance, but the paper's framing is bias detection, not values alignment. High A4 conflation score.

assessments.filename: 2021-Mohit Chandra-Subverting the Jewtocracy Online Antisemitism Detection.md

features.B3_note: Judaism treated as a monolithic target of hate speech; no theological engagement
features.Q1_metric: Multiple annotators with scheme; specific agreement metric in paper

assessments.assessor_notes: This is a multimodal antisemitism detection system using Twitter and Gab data (3,102 + 3,509 posts). It tests whether models can detect antisemitic content using text and images. This has ZERO relevance to religious values testing -- it is purely a hate speech detection task where Judaism is the target of abuse, not the subject of values assessment. A3 is near-zero; A4 bias-values conflation is 95 because this is entirely about detecting bias AGAINST a religious group, which is categorically different from testing alignment WITH religious values. The highest conflation score in the batch.

features.B3_note: Specifically Advaita Vedanta school; acknowledges it is one school within Hindu philosophy
features.Q1_metric: Human evaluations by computational linguists and domain experts

assessments.assessor_notes: VedantaNY-10M is a RAG dataset curated from public discourses on Advaita Vedanta, an ancient Indian philosophical tradition. This is one of the most genuinely religiously-engaged benchmarks in the batch. It tests whether RAG models can accurately answer questions about Vedantic philosophy, which inherently involves values and metaphysical concepts. The dataset comes from actual philosophical discourses, and the evaluation uses domain experts. A3 is moderate-high because while the task is QA (knowledge-like), the content domain is deeply philosophical and values-laden. The paper won Outstanding Paper Award at ACL 2024 ML4AL Workshop. Notably specific to one school (Advaita Vedanta) within Hinduism, showing commendable denominational specificity.

assessments.filename: 2025-Zhou-WYWEB A NLP Evaluation Benchmark For Classical Chinese.md

features.B3_note: Classical Chinese texts span Confucian, Buddhist, Taoist traditions but treated as undifferentiated 'classical Chinese'

assessments.assessor_notes: WYWEB is a general NLP benchmark for Classical Chinese (wen yan wen) with 9 tasks including sentence classification, sequence labeling, reading comprehension, and machine translation. The religious connection is incidental -- Classical Chinese literature includes Buddhist sutras, Confucian classics, and Taoist texts, but WYWEB treats them as a language domain, not a religious domain. The benchmark tests NLP capabilities on classical language, not religious values understanding. A3 is low because the religious content is a byproduct of the literary corpus, not the evaluation target. High floor effect risk because existing PLMs struggle with Classical Chinese.

assessments.filename: 2024-Cao-C3Bench A Comprehensive Classical Chinese Understanding Benchmark for.md

features.B3_note: 10 domains of classical Chinese but treated as unified language comprehension task

assessments.assessor_notes: C3Bench has 50,000 text pairs across 5 CCU tasks (classification, retrieval, NER, punctuation, translation) from 10 domains of classical Chinese. Like WYWEB, the religious content is incidental to the language comprehension focus. The benchmark explicitly positions itself as testing language understanding capabilities, not values or religious knowledge. Data spans all of classical Chinese literature, which includes philosophical and religious texts but is not limited to them. A3 is low for the same reasons as WYWEB. Existing LLMs 'struggle with CCU tasks and still inferior to supervised models' -- high floor risk.

features.B3_note: Single tradition (Islam); 32 reciters capture stylistic diversity but not denominational diversity

assessments.assessor_notes: QURAN-MD is a multimodal dataset integrating textual, linguistic, and audio dimensions of the Quran at verse and word levels. It includes 32 reciters' audio, Arabic text, English translations, transliteration, morphological analysis, and word-level audio alignment. This is a RESOURCE dataset, not a values benchmark. It supports ASR, TTS, tajweed detection, and linguistic analysis -- all technical NLP/speech tasks. The Quran content is inherently value-laden, but the dataset's purpose is enabling computational processing of sacred text, not testing values alignment. A3 is low because the intended downstream tasks are technical (speech recognition, text-to-speech), not values-oriented. Published at NeurIPS 2025 Datasets track.
